data.title: Sučany – Skala, a hillfort on a 40 m crag
data.excerpt: In the village of Sučany a 40 m high rocky crag called Skala rises up – the last spur of the Fatra range and, in Janšák's words, a terrain so perfect that no more ideal natural castle could be imagined. Three ramparts, Púchov and Slavic sherds, Roman coins and two 14th-century forgeries show how often the place was put to use.
data.metaTitle: Sučany – Skala, a hillfort on a 40 m crag
data.metaDescription: A hillfort on the 40 m high Skala crag at Sučany, the last spur of the Fatra, where nature itself provided an almost impregnable promontory.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: The Skala hillfort lies in the village of Sučany on a 40 m high rocky crag, the last spur of the Bukovina ridge (spot height 538) in the Fatra range.

keyFacts.label: Natural defences
keyFacts.value: Skala was separated from the ridge by a natural step 8 m high; on the south and west it is bounded by almost vertical, overhanging rock faces, on the north by a slope of 45 degrees.

keyFacts.label: The three ramparts
keyFacts.value: The hillfort was protected by three ramparts: the circuit rampart k–b–z–i–l, 94 m long, the rampart m–o–c–s–n, 88 m long, and the outer, almost semicircular rampart o–p–d–r–s, 108 m long.

keyFacts.label: Height of the ramparts
keyFacts.value: The rampart m–o–c–s–n reaches a height of 8 m towards the hillfort and 4 m in the opposite direction; the highest point of the rampart o–p–d–r–s rises 6 m above the bottom of the adjoining ditch.

keyFacts.label: Area of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: The inhabited plateau of the hillfort covered 4,350 m² and was horseshoe-shaped.

keyFacts.label: Archaeological finds
keyFacts.value: The hillfort yielded Slavic sherds with wavy-line decoration, wheel-thrown Púchov sherds, daub, a clay bead, two bronze brooches of the 1st century AD and the remains of semi-sunken buildings with post construction.

keyFacts.label: Coins and striking
keyFacts.value: The finds include two forged coins of the 14th century, a copper blank perhaps prepared for counterfeit striking, a coin of the Cotini and several Roman coins.

keyFacts.label: Researchers
keyFacts.value: The hillfort was investigated by Štefan Janšák (1930), Igor Hrubec (excavations in the 1950s and 1960s, published in SA 1961) and A. Petrovský-Šichman (VZP 1964).

timeline.title: Occupation in the Roman period
timeline.description: Two bronze brooches dated to the 1st century AD were found at the hillfort, which attests occupation of the plateau in this period as well.

timeline.year: the period of the Púchov culture
timeline.title: Occupation during the Púchov culture
timeline.description: The remains of semi-sunken buildings with post construction and a quantity of Púchov culture sherds attest occupation of the hillfort in this period.

timeline.title: Forged coins and striking
timeline.description: Two coins of the 14th century, which Janšák identified as forgeries, were found at the hillfort, as well as a circular copper blank perhaps prepared for counterfeit striking.

timeline.title: The first survey and description of the hillfort (Janšák)
timeline.description: Štefan Janšák was the first to survey the hillfort and publish it; he stated that there could be no more perfect natural castle than Skala itself.

timeline.title: Igor Hrubec's excavations
timeline.description: Igor Hrubec carried out archaeological excavations at Sučany, in the course of which he established that occupation of the hillfort was always linked to a settlement lying to the north of it, towards the Váh.

timeline.title: Publication of the excavation in Slovenská archeológia
timeline.description: Igor Hrubec published the results of his investigation of the hillfort in the journal Slovenská archeológia (volume 9, pp. 209 – 215).

timeline.title: A. Petrovský-Šichman's find and publication
timeline.description: A. Petrovský-Šichman managed to record and publish several Slavic sherds with wavy-line decoration from the hillfort (VZP 1964).

children.text: In the village of Sučany a 40 m high rocky crag called Skala rises up, which is interesting from the geographical and geological point of view as well as the historical. It is the last spur of the much and variously dissected Fatra massif, in fact of its low Bukovina ridge (spot height 538), which runs from Sučany and the Štiavnička stream towards Martin.

“Skala” forms an ideal terrain for founding a hillfort on a mountain promontory. The natural position offers such advantages that the first inhabitant needed no artificial fortification, because Skala was separated from the ridge by a natural step 8 m high. On the south and west the plateau is bounded by almost vertical, indeed overhanging rock faces, on the north by a slope of 45 degrees. Janšák, who was the first to survey the hillfort and publish it in 1930, states that there could be no more perfect natural castle than Skala itself. Access to it was only along the ridge. Contact with the nearest running water, as well as the descent to the lowland on which the hillfort depended economically, was provided by a path that still survived in the 1930s.

children.text: The artificial defences, which by their purposeful construction and arrangement increase the natural security, make this hillfort almost impregnable in times when siege technology was very imperfect. The circuit rampart k–b–z–i–l runs in an arc for a length of 94 m along the edge of the plateau wherever there is no rock. Today it is already considerably flattened, barely 0.30 – 0.40 m high; in the stretch e–j it has completely collapsed and slid down the slope. Far more pronounced and better preserved is the second rampart m–o–c–s–n, which joins the rock at point m at spot height 423 and from there climbs in an arc to a height of 432, and towards the north-west descends again to spot height 422 at point n, with a total length of 88 m. Finally there is the outer, almost semicircular rampart o–p–d–r–s, beginning at spot height 428 at point o, climbing to a height of 434 and descending back to the 424 contour, to point s. Its length reaches 108 m. The height of the rampart m–o–c–s–n reaches 8 m towards the hillfort (between point y and spot height 432), and 4 m in the opposite direction. The highest point of the rampart o–p–d–r–s, namely spot height 434, rises 6 m above the bottom of the adjoining ditch. The material from which the ramparts were built was obtained on the spot, namely by digging deep ditches.

The once inhabited plateau of the hillfort, with an area of 4,350 m², is horseshoe-shaped and is at the same time its only enclosure. The spaces between the ramparts m–c–h, o–d–s and the rock massif are not suitable for habitation because of their very small size and the excessive differences in height between the individual parts. The summit plateau on the rock, on the other hand, made up in quality for any shortcomings in size. It is a sloping little plain, descending regularly from east to west, with a small conical projection on the south-eastern side. Janšák states that this projection may have served as a pagan sacrificial site.

children.text: At the hillfort Janšák found several Slavic sherds with wavy-line decoration, wheel-thrown Púchov sherds, daub and also a clay bead of red colour. An interesting find was two coins of the 14th century, which Janšák identified as forgeries, and also a circular copper blank prepared for (perhaps counterfeit) striking. Igor Hrubec, who carried out archaeological excavations at Sučany in the 1950s and 1960s (SA 1961), states that occupation of the hillfort was always linked to a settlement that lay to the north of it, towards the Váh. Besides many Púchov culture sherds, he also found Slavic sherds. Similarly, A. Petrovský-Šichman also managed to record and publish several Slavic sherds with wavy-line decoration (VZP 1964). Hrubec also mentions finds of a coin of the Cotini and of several Roman coins from the site. He also found two bronze brooches dated to the 1st century AD and the remains of semi-sunken buildings with post construction, likewise dated to the period of the Púchov culture.
